title: Prompt Caching
shortDefinition: A technique for storing and reusing LLM responses for repeated inputs, significantly reducing API costs and latency.
definition: Prompt caching is a technique for storing and reusing LLM responses (or intermediate computation results) for repeated or similar inputs, rather than generating a fresh response from the model for every single request — significantly reducing both API cost and response latency for high-volume applications where many requests involve the same or similar prompt content. Many providers now offer native prompt caching features that automatically cache computation from repeated prompt prefixes at the infrastructure level.

sections.title: How prompt caching works
sections.description: Application-level caching stores complete responses; provider-level caching caches intermediate computation for repeated prompt prefixes.

content.text: At the application level, caching stores the complete model response to a specific input and returns it directly for subsequent identical requests without making another API call — effective when many users ask the same question. At the infrastructure level, providers like Anthropic offer 'context caching' that caches intermediate computation results for repeated prompt prefixes (like a long system prompt or large document context that appears in every request) — the provider charges reduced rates for processing cached tokens, since the computation was already done. Both forms meaningfully reduce cost and latency for applications with significant prompt repetition.

items: Application-level caching — store complete responses for identical requests.
Provider-level caching — cache intermediate computation for repeated prompt prefixes.
Reduced token charges — providers charge less for cached computation.
Cost and latency reduction — meaningful for applications with repetition.
Two forms — complementary, both reduce cost and latency.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Prompt caching avoids redundant generation — it stores and reuses responses or computation, saving both time and money.

sections.title: Where prompt caching has the most impact
sections.description: Caching delivers the greatest benefit when prompt content has high repetition.

content.text: Prompt caching delivers the greatest benefit when prompt content has high repetition — applications with a fixed, lengthy system prompt sent with every request (the system prompt computation can be cached), RAG systems where the same document is referenced in many queries, customer-facing FAQ systems where many users ask equivalent questions, and any application where identical or very similar requests are common. Applications with highly unique, custom inputs from every user have less opportunity for effective caching, though even caching the static system prompt portion can meaningfully reduce per-request cost.

items: Fixed system prompts — lengthy prompts repeated with every request.
RAG systems — same documents referenced across many queries.
FAQ systems — many users asking equivalent questions.
Unique inputs — less caching opportunity for highly custom requests.
Partial benefit — even caching the static portion reduces cost.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of prompt caching

content.text: Prompt caching has limitations. It only reduces costs when there is repetition in prompt content. Managing cache invalidation adds complexity to applications, and stale responses can be returned if the TTL is too long for your use case. Provider-level caching may not be available for all providers or models, and implementation adds operational complexity. Caching may reduce cost but does not improve the model's capabilities, and measuring actual cost savings requires good monitoring infrastructure.

items: Repetition dependency — only helps when prompts are repeated.
Cache invalidation complexity — managing TTLs adds operational overhead.
Stale response risk — outdated content if not invalidated appropriately.
Provider availability — not all providers offer infrastructure-level caching.
No capability improvement — caching doesn't improve model quality.
Monitoring required — need good infrastructure to measure savings.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about prompt caching

items.question: Does prompt caching affect response quality?
items.answer: No — caching returns the exact same model response that was generated on the first request; it doesn't alter model behavior, only eliminates redundant generation for identical inputs.

items.question: Can prompt caching work for personalized responses, or only generic ones?
items.answer: Application-level response caching works best for responses that genuinely should be the same for all users asking a particular question; provider-level prefix caching can be valuable even for personalized applications if a common prompt prefix (like a long system prompt or shared document context) appears in every request.

items.question: How do you measure whether caching is actually working and reducing costs?
items.answer: Through monitoring of cache hit rates and API cost comparison before and after implementation — ClickMasters builds this measurement as part of any caching implementation.

items.question: Can caching be used alongside streaming responses?
items.answer: Application-level response caching and streaming are harder to combine (since caching stores complete responses while streaming delivers them incrementally); provider-level prefix caching is compatible with streaming since it caches computation rather than final responses.

items.question: How long does implementing prompt caching take?
items.answer: 4–14 weeks depending on application complexity and whether this is caching alone or part of a broader cost optimization engagement.

items.question: Should we cache all LLM responses, or only specific ones?
items.answer: ClickMasters designs selective caching strategies that cache where repetition is high and freshness requirements allow, rather than blanket caching of all responses regardless of how unique or time-sensitive they are.

items.question: What is the difference between application-level and provider-level caching?
items.answer: Application-level caching stores complete responses at your application layer. Provider-level caching caches intermediate computation results (like prompt prefixes) at the provider's infrastructure, reducing token processing costs. Both can be used together.

items.question: How does prompt caching interact with rate limits?
items.answer: Caching reduces the number of API calls, which can help you stay within rate limits. This is particularly valuable for high-volume applications that might otherwise hit rate limiting thresholds.

items.question: What is a cache hit rate and what is considered good?
items.answer: Cache hit rate is the percentage of requests served from cache rather than generating a new response. A good hit rate depends on your application — 50% or higher can yield significant savings. ClickMasters helps you optimize for your specific pattern.

items.question: Can caching be combined with model routing for cost optimization?
items.answer: Yes — caching and model routing are complementary cost optimization strategies. Caching reduces redundant generation, while routing directs simpler queries to cheaper models. ClickMasters combines both for maximum cost efficiency.
